summary: A short note on how to write math-like descriptions in specifications. When a function uses two formulas for adjoining domains but is continuous at the boundary, the author describes it in a particular form. It also replaces the correction in RFC 132 and updates RFC 107.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 154 recommends a way to write a function that uses one formula on each side of a boundary. The formulas both include the boundary, where they have the same value, so the overlap does not make the definition ambiguous.

subtitle: A short note on writing two formulas for a continuous piecewise function.

tldr.problem: A function may need two formulas on adjoining domains even though it is continuous at their shared boundary.
tldr.mechanism: The note writes one formula for x less than or equal to a and another for x greater than or equal to a.
tldr.outcome: The domains overlap at a, but the note says there is no ambiguity because f1(a) equals f2(a). RFC 154 obsoletes RFC 132 and updates RFC 107.

sections.title: A Function with Two Formulas
sections.content:
The note describes a function that needs two formulas, f1 and f2, on adjoining domains. The function is continuous at the boundary point a.

It presents a graph in which the function changes at a while remaining continuous there.
sections.plainLanguage: Some functions use one formula on one side of a boundary and a different formula on the other. This note explains how to write that definition.

sections.title: The Suggested Notation
sections.content:
The suggested form is f(x) = f1(x) for x <= a, and f(x) = f2(x) for x >= a. Both conditions include the boundary point a.

The RFC observes that a careful reader will notice the domains overlap at that point.
sections.plainLanguage: Write the first rule for values up to and including a. Write the second rule for values from a onward.

sections.title: Why the Overlap Is Unambiguous
sections.content:
Two formulas can overlap at a only if they give the same value there. The note states that f1(a) = f2(a).

Because both formulas agree at the shared boundary, the note says the overlap creates no semantic ambiguity.
sections.plainLanguage: At the shared point, both rules give the same answer. A reader can use either rule there without getting a different value.
